study: Does real memory latency favour the pipeline over the single-cycle core?
answer: No. The hypothesis was wrong and is recorded as such.
benchmark: hello.c, 297 instructions, both cores verified against Spike at every point
note: LATENCY counts wait states, so an access costs LATENCY+1 cycles. Both the instruction and data ports use the same value. LATENCY=0 reproduces magic_mem exactly and is the control.
prediction: That the single-cycle core would degrade faster, because it must fetch an instruction AND access data within one instruction, while a pipeline has them in separate stages that overlap.
outcome: The penalty flattens at 29% and never closes. Memory latency hurts both cores by the same factor, so the pipeline keeps its hazard overhead as pure loss.
root_cause: There is no fetch buffer. An instruction-fetch stall freezes the whole pipeline, so fetch latency is serialised per instruction exactly as it is on the single-cycle core. The stages cannot overlap what the front end will not decouple. The single-cycle core also gets a break the model gives for free: its instruction and data accesses use two independent ports whose counters run concurrently, so at 1 wait state it costs 2 cycles per instruction rather than 4.
what_would_actually_change_it: An instruction cache, or even a small prefetch buffer, so IF can run ahead while MEM is blocked. That is the missing piece, not more pipeline stages. This result is the argument FOR building one.
still_unmeasured: What putting memory inside the synthesised path does to Fmax. magic_mem and latency_mem are both simulation-only and excluded from synthesis, so the claim that a single-cycle core cannot fit fetch plus data access into one clock period remains untested here. Cycle counts say nothing about it either way.
